# A virtual store: BRAN on THREDDS {#sec-virtual}

```{r}
#| include: false
source("R/book.R")
```

Most of the world's gridded data is not Zarr and will not be rewritten as
Zarr. It is NetCDF and HDF5, in archives, served as files. A *virtual*
Zarr store leaves those files alone and keeps a table of references: for
each chunk, which file, which byte offset, how many bytes. Kerchunk and
VirtualiZarr write such tables; zaro reads them (kerchunk JSON and
Parquet, VirtualiZarr Parquet manifests, byterefs tables) and from then on
the store behaves like any other.

BRAN is CSIRO's Bluelink ocean reanalysis: daily fields at 51 depths on a
0.1 degree global grid, as monthly NetCDF files on NCI's THREDDS server
(BRAN2020 to 2009, BRAN2023 from 2010). Reference stores for it, one per
variable and each in several forms, are published
[on Source Cooperative](https://source.coop/ausantarctic/ausantarctic-scratch/bluelink),
built with [raad.virtualize](https://github.com/mdsumner/raad.virtualize).
Temperature is one array of 3600 x 1500 x 51 x 12265 values, every day
from 1993, in chunks of 300 x 300 x 1 x 1: each chunk is a tile of one
depth on one day, a few tens of kilobytes inside a monthly NetCDF file.
That is 37.5 million chunks, and the table that locates them is itself
read lazily, a few row groups at a time.

```r
bran <- zaro("flatrefs://https://data.source.coop/ausantarctic/ausantarctic-scratch/bluelink/bluelink-daily-temp/flat",
             target = "public")
temp <- zaro_array(bran, "temp", cf = TRUE)    # degrees C
dim(temp)
#> [1]  3600  1500    51 12265
```

No NetCDF library is involved, and nothing is copied. The references
name the files as they sit on NCI's disks; `target = "public"` maps them
to their THREDDS addresses.

## The reads

A surface map for one day (60 chunks, all in one file); a profile at one
cell (51 chunks, one per depth); a north-south section by depth; and a
month of surface values at one cell.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
#| file: scripts/04-virtual.R
```

```{r}
res <- book_run("04-virtual.R", live = TRUE)
book_table(res)
```

This store shows something the native Zarr store could not. When zaro is
given a whole batch, it looks at the byte ranges, and ranges that touch in
the same file are merged into one request. The 60 tiles of a surface map
sit end to end in the NetCDF file, so a planned read of the map can be a
single HTTP request. Asked one chunk at a time, there is nothing to merge:
60 requests to a THREDDS server, in series. (Reads from THREDDS in this
book are capped at 4 concurrent requests; the server resets connections
not far above that.)

So here the **Requests** column can differ between builds, while **MB**
stays the same. Fewer, larger requests are kinder to an archive server
than many small ones, as well as faster for the reader. The patch is what
lets R be the polite client.

```{r}
book_elt(res)
```

::: {.callout-note}
If the stock column says "failed", that is a result too. On the first
three renders of this chapter, from a GitHub runner on 2026-11-21 and 22,
the patched build completed every read, and the stock build completed
none: each attempt ended with the server resetting a connection, and the
same happened from Pawsey. (Those renders read an earlier reference store
for the same files.) The
likely cause is the rate of new connections. On stock R every chunk is
its own fetch call, and zaro opens a new connection for each call, so 60
small chunks are 60 TLS handshakes in quick succession. The same stock
loop against the same server in @sec-icechunk, at a slower pace, went
through. Keeping connections open between fetch calls would help zaro
here; asking once is what removes the problem.
:::

## A track is already fine

One read from this store needs no patch: values along a track, one
(x, y, depth, day) per row, is a matrix subscript (@sec-points). A 30-day
track off Tasmania was 30 byte ranges from 30 files, one fetch call, 2 MB
in half a second (measured 2026-10-03). The profile and the section above
are the same data asked for as rectangles, and that is the only reason
they fare differently.
